title: Indicating Resolver Support of DNSSEC
summary: Proposes using a bit in the EDNS0 header, the DO bit, so a resolver can say it understands DNSSEC records. Servers then add DNSSEC data to responses only when asked. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Some people do not want extra paperwork with their answer. This is a small checkbox in a question that says that the asker can handle the extra security details.

questions: how does a resolver signal dnssec support
what is the dnssec ok bit
what does the do bit do in dns
why does dnssec cause tcp fallback
subtitle: A single flag bit in the EDNS0 header lets a resolver tell a DNS server it can accept DNSSEC records.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC-aware servers would send bulky security records to every client, including ones that do not understand them, causing truncated UDP responses, TCP retries and, in reported cases, failing resolvers.
tldr.mechanism: The resolver sets the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit, the most significant bit of the Z field in the EDNS0 OPT record, and the server includes SIG, KEY and NXT records only when that bit is set.
tldr.outcome: Servers add DNSSEC data only when asked, which avoids the operational cost for non-DNSSEC clients. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

facts.label: Flag position
facts.value: Most significant bit of the Z field in the EDNS0 OPT record

today: RFC 3225 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2001, and it has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. Read those updates alongside it for the current DNSSEC rules.

sections.title: Why Servers Need to Be Told
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS data. A DNSSEC-aware server answering for a signed zone responds with SIG, KEY and/or NXT records. This RFC calls these the DNSSEC security RRs.

Early on, most queries will come from resolvers that know nothing about DNSSEC. Sending them the extra records can have significant negative operational impacts for the DNS infrastructure, so the RFC says a server should send them only when the resolver explicitly indicates it can understand them.
sections.eli5: Imagine a librarian who staples a thick stack of extra forms to every answer. Most visitors only wanted the answer, so the librarian should ask first.

sections.title: The Cost of Unwanted Security Records
sections.content:
DNS UDP datagrams are limited to 512 bytes. Responses carrying DNSSEC security RRs therefore have a high probability of being truncated, which makes the resolver retry over TCP.

The RFC expects the TCP retries to be quite detrimental: typically five packets for a single query and response instead of two, extra latency from additional round trips, more queries failing from timeouts, and significantly increased load on nameservers.

It also notes reports from preliminary and experimental DNSSEC deployment of non-DNSSEC-aware resolvers that could not handle such responses. In the worst case the resolver failed, and in the better case the whole response was ignored.
sections.eli5: Extra forms make the answer too big for a postcard, so the asker has to go and fetch it in a big box instead. That takes longer and wears everyone out.

sections.title: Choosing a Bit in the EDNS0 Header
sections.content:
The RFC assumes client support for DNSSEC is binary: the client will either accept all DNSSEC security RRs or none. A single bit is enough to say which.

The bit lives in the EDNS0 header rather than the classic DNS header. Bits in the classic header are scarce, and non-compliant caching or forwarding servers might inappropriately copy data from classic headers when passing queries on to authoritative servers.

The RFC also considers and rejects an alternative: treating the mere presence of an EDNS0 header as an implicit sign of DNSSEC support. That was not chosen because some applications support EDNS0 but should not use DNSSEC.
sections.eli5: Instead of squeezing a tick box onto a crowded form, the designers put it on the roomy extra page. Just having the extra page does not count as saying yes.

sections.title: The DO Bit and Server Behavior
sections.content:
The DNSSEC OK (DO) bit is the most significant bit of the Z field in the EDNS0 OPT record of the query. It is the first bit of the third and fourth bytes of the extended RCODE and flags portion.

When DO is one, the resolver can accept DNSSEC security RRs. When it is zero, those RRs MUST NOT be returned unless they are explicitly queried for. The DO bit of the query MUST be copied in the response. Security records that match an explicit SIG, KEY, NXT or ANY query, or that are part of the zone data for an AXFR or IXFR query, are included whether or not DO was set.

A recursive DNSSEC-aware server MUST set DO on its own recursive requests, whatever the initiating resolver sent. If the initiating request did not have DO set, the server MUST remove the security RRs before replying, but cached data MUST NOT be modified.

If a server answers a DO query with NOTIMP, FORMERR or SERVFAIL, the resolver SHOULD NOT expect DNSSEC security RRs and SHOULD retry without EDNS0, as described in section 5.3 of RFC 2671.
sections.eli5: If the question has the box ticked, the answer comes with the extra forms. If it is not ticked, the forms stay behind, unless you asked for them by name. A middleman who talks to the boss always ticks the box, then removes the forms before handing you the answer.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The absence of DNSSEC data in a response to a query with DO set MUST NOT be taken to mean that no security information is available for that zone. The response may be forged, or it may be a non-forged response to an altered query with the bit cleared.

For IANA, RFC 2671 defines 16 bits of extended flags in the OPT record, encoded in its TTL field. This RFC reserves one of them as the OK bit and requests that the left most bit be allocated.
sections.eli5: If the extra forms are missing, you cannot assume nothing was signed. Someone along the way might have faked the answer or removed the tick from your question.
